And you had to play a melody for them people to know what I was playing. I couldn't just sit there and vary it.
Yeah.

That's how I learned how to pick up melody. I used to play three piece job. I used to play them kind of numbers with three pieces. Let's see if I can take a look. Remember that go from Hagen? Oh yeah.
I used to play that with three pieces all the way. That's the introduction I made that just now.
Why don't you make that just now?
Why don't you make that just now? Why don't you make that stuff . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

There's one other question about your brother, you know on the trumpet like Armstrong he shakes his hand sort of like that. Well that's the sort of a trill, yeah. Do you ever do that on the clarinet? Yeah, that's the sort of a trill. Gives it a little sort of a trilling effect.
Yeah, it gives a little sort of a trilling effect.
Yeah, you consciously shake your arm a little bit.
Yeah, that gives it a trilling effect. So, uh...

segments.title: Arrival and the Laurents' new house
segments.summary: Russell settles in at Laurent's house, which he bought after his wife lost her legs and could not manage the stairs of the old upstairs flat.

segments.title: Name, pronunciation and birth date
segments.summary: Laurent gives his full name, how Laurent is pronounced, and his birth on 28 August 1897, St. Augustine's day.

segments.title: Growing up in the 7th Ward among the Tios, Picou and Big Eye
segments.summary: He was born at Prairie and La Perouse and lists which street corners Big Eye Louis, Picou and the Tios lived on.

segments.title: Violin at nine, then piano with his sister
segments.summary: He started on violin, disliked it, took piano at twelve with his sister, and gave it up for his father's trade.

segments.title: Roofing trade and buying a clarinet to take lessons
segments.summary: Working as a roofer with his father, he is urged to get a clarinet, buys one and starts fingering lessons, playing in about six months.

segments.chapter: Clarinet fingering and the Tio family
segments.title: Freak fingering for C sharp and B flat on the Albert system
segments.summary: He explains the Albert-system clarinet and the unusual alternate fingerings he learned for C sharp and B flat, and a player who plugged broken keys with cork.

segments.chapter: Clarinet fingering and the Tio family
segments.title: Tio's patched-up clarinet and the trip to New York
segments.summary: His wife is introduced; Laurent recalls a great clarinetist whose clarinet was held with rubber bands and cork and who was told to buy a new one before a New York trip.

segments.chapter: Clarinet fingering and the Tio family
segments.title: Why a player must keep practising
segments.summary: He says music stays with you only if you play daily; after five years off his fingers, lips and breath control have suffered.

segments.chapter: Clarinet fingering and the Tio family
segments.title: The Tio family: Papa Tio, Lorenzo and their origins
segments.summary: Papa Tio was the greatest clarinetist of his day and young Lorenzo came up under him; Laurent speculates the family was French or Mexican, and notes the Tranchina's job.

segments.chapter: Clarinet fingering and the Tio family
segments.title: Working a day trade and playing all night
segments.summary: He recalls roofing by day, playing until three or four in the morning, and transposing piano copies into parts.

segments.chapter: Clarinet fingering and the Tio family
segments.title: Method books and continued lessons with several teachers
segments.summary: He used the Klose method and others, and kept taking lessons with his sister, Lorenzo Tio, Papa Tio and another teacher.

segments.title: Playing with Charlie McCurdy's band
segments.summary: Shortly before McCurdy's death he played clarinet and soprano in a band with violin, trumpet, alto, Helen Edwards on piano and a drummer.

segments.title: Photograph with Dr. Bechet in 1935
segments.summary: Russell and Laurent discuss the large picture of Laurent with Dr. Bechet, taken in the dentist's parlor.

segments.title: Photograph of Laurent's band with Picou
segments.summary: Laurent names the musicians in the band picture, including Picou, a trumpeter, Billy Pierce at piano, Fan Bourgeois, a trombonist and Albert Francis on drums.

segments.title: The two records cut at the hall and lost from the car
segments.summary: His band cut two numbers on a home recording machine, and the only copies were stolen from his car seat.

segments.title: His copyrighted compositions
segments.summary: He shows copyrighted songs such as I Got a Woman Doing What You Used to Do and says he never had time to publish or record them.

segments.chapter: Lessons with Papa Tio and Helen Edwards
segments.title: Papa Tio's strict lessons, fees and teaching method
segments.summary: Papa Tio sent pupils home if they had not learned the lesson, charged Laurent fifty cents against two dollars from white pupils, and taught counting and solfege.

segments.chapter: Lessons with Papa Tio and Helen Edwards
segments.title: Helen Edwards, the pianist who transposed at sight
segments.summary: Pianist Helen Edwards, who died in California, could transpose any song for a singer; her sister read better than Billy.

segments.chapter: Arrangements, repertoire and the last band
segments.title: Manuscripts and arrangements he wrote for his band
segments.summary: He shows parts he wrote, buying piano copies and arranging them for every instrument, and recalls popular tunes he played, including a three-piece band that played Copenhagen.

segments.chapter: Arrangements, repertoire and the last band
segments.title: Sadie, the Fosters and a run of tunes he played
segments.summary: A short exchange about the drummer married to Billy's sister, followed by Laurent reeling off waltzes and popular songs from his books.

segments.chapter: Arrangements, repertoire and the last band
segments.title: Instructing a police-band saxophonist during Prohibition
segments.summary: At Bernard's during Prohibition a police corporal came nightly for sax instruction and tips and brought a piano copy Laurent turned into a band number.

segments.chapter: Arrangements, repertoire and the last band
segments.title: More songs from the books, Copenhagen and Chinaman and Mabel
segments.summary: Laurent names more tunes, recites the words of Chinaman and Mabel, which he says he never copyrighted, and says he used to sing choruses.

segments.chapter: Arrangements, repertoire and the last band
segments.title: His last band with Charlie Love's books and Humphrey
segments.summary: The trumpet books were last used by Charlie Love; the final band at Happy Landing included old man Humphrey, who then had a stroke and lost a leg.

segments.chapter: Arrangements, repertoire and the last band
segments.title: Fats Domino's brother-in-law and the lost bag of orchestrations
segments.summary: Laurent complains about a pianist who will not hire the brother-in-law who taught him, and tells of leaving $200 of orchestrations on a streetcar.

segments.chapter: Arrangements, repertoire and the last band
segments.title: Piano players and trombonists in his last band
segments.summary: He names pianists Odette Davis, Walter Decou and George Decou, and asks about trombone in the band.

segments.chapter: Arrangements, repertoire and the last band
segments.title: Rickard Alexis and Buddy Petit losing work by taking multiple deposits
segments.summary: Laurent says Rickard Alexis and Buddy Petit lost jobs, including the Roosevelt, because they took several deposits for the same night.

segments.chapter: Clarinetists, brass bands and the day job
segments.title: Big Eye Louis and the C versus B flat clarinet
segments.summary: Big Eye played C clarinet most of his life and mastered it better than B flat, though local players mostly used B flat and E flat.

segments.chapter: Clarinetists, brass bands and the day job
segments.title: Never marching: carnival floats only
segments.summary: He never played a funeral or parade on foot, only on carnival floats, because he disliked walking.

segments.chapter: Clarinetists, brass bands and the day job
segments.title: Letter carrier in 1919 and earnings at the roofing trade
segments.summary: He carried mail for eighteen months, quit in 1919 for the roofing trade, whose pay rose far past the post office's, and he now owns rental property.

segments.chapter: Clarinetists, brass bands and the day job
segments.title: Big Eye and Picou as music readers
segments.summary: Big Eye did not read music and Laurent helped him; Picou could read, though not brilliantly.

segments.title: The 1949 jazz meeting and the High Society question
segments.summary: At a National Jazz meeting on Carondelet Street Laurent and others were asked who originated the High Society variation, and he took George Baquet and others to the meeting.

segments.title: George Baquet explains the flute-part variation
segments.summary: At the meeting records were played, Baquet did not recognise himself, and he said the variation came from a flute part transposed for clarinet, not from Picou.

segments.title: Neighbours of his boyhood and where musicians lived
segments.summary: Old man Glenn, Joe Brown and Manuel Perez lived near him, and he cannot place George Field's residence.

segments.title: McCurdy, Picou and the flute-part story told again
segments.summary: Asked about McCurdy, Laurent repeats the Baquet account, set on an out-of-town job, and recalls playing duets with Picou in a backyard.

segments.title: Picou's clarinets and Laurent's own clarinets with rings
segments.summary: They compare Picou's straight wooden clarinet with the ring-less and ring-equipped clarinets Laurent has owned and kept.

segments.title: Valette clarinet and the instruments he sold
segments.summary: He shows a Paris-made Valette clarinet, describes his decorated clarinet that Willie Humphrey wanted, and the pencil model he sold.

segments.title: Reeds and embouchure
segments.summary: He explains the reed strengths he now uses and how he keeps his upper lip even with the teeth with pressure on the lip.

segments.title: Bernard's Cafe, the camp and Al Capone's tips
segments.summary: He played five and a half years at Michel Bernard's cabaret, once at Capone's camp, and recalls huge tips and Capone's wallet.

segments.title: Laurent tries to play a number
segments.summary: Laurent attempts to play a number on the clarinet, tires, and mentions the many orchestrations he kept by the piano.

segments.title: Embouchure learned from Lorenzo Tio, and how others held the lip
segments.summary: He got his embouchure from Tio, does not bite the lip, and says Papa Tio held his lip the same while Big Eye bit down.

segments.title: Playing fill-ins and an old number
segments.summary: Laurent plays fill-in variations and a Richard M. Jones number and says he loses numbers sometimes.

segments.title: Vibrato and endurance
segments.summary: He says vibrato is made by moving tension in the lips, not the throat, and that he never tired on a job.

segments.title: Sam Dutrey as an improviser
segments.summary: The elder Sam Dutrey was a great improviser who held his lip like Lorenzo Tio.

segments.title: Fragmentary tape passage
segments.summary: Brief garbled stretch with a name repeated and a goodbye.

segments.title: Johnny St. Cyr in his band and playing with Manetta
segments.summary: Johnny St. Cyr played guitar in Laurent's band after returning from playing with Louis; he never played jobs with Professor Manetta.

segments.title: Lorenzo Tio as the greatest clarinetist
segments.summary: Laurent says no clarinetist could be greater than Lorenzo, who excelled at jazz, opera and brass band, playing E flat on parade.

segments.title: Tio's night-band lineup and today's clarinetists
segments.summary: He lists the Tio and Bocage lineup with Piron and the old men, then tries to name young white clarinetists such as Pete Fountain.

segments.title: Committing music to memory
segments.summary: He used to memorise a song in ten minutes from a copy but says it is slipping now.

segments.title: Playing and singing, and hot choruses
segments.summary: Laurent plays a song, sings a lyric, and talks about hot choruses.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet as a boy and his return
segments.summary: Bechet grew up near Laurent, began on a cheap flute, played for a dollar a night, and later sold tunes for whiskey; Laurent met him at the airport.

segments.title: Waltzes and the Joplin rag book
segments.summary: Laurent and Russell look through his waltzes and a rag book that Charlie Love used to play, and Laurent says he played from memory.

segments.title: Laurent's recent composition and Petite Fleur
segments.summary: He shows a number composed last summer in Chicago, and Petite Fleur is discussed as Bechet's last hit.

segments.title: Writing arrangements and eyesight
segments.summary: He wrote parts for the band by day, and the group chat about not needing eyeglasses and relatives who read without them.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet's falling-out with his brother
segments.summary: Sidney and his brother Dr. Bechet became bitter, and Sidney stayed ragged with only his flute and clarinet.

segments.title: The cousin who gave Louis Armstrong his first trumpet
segments.summary: Laurent says his cousin, in charge of boys at the Home, gave Louis Armstrong his first trumpet, and mentions a violinist cousin.

segments.title: Where Bechet lived and his first trip back in twenty years
segments.summary: He lists Bechet's addresses and says his brother only became proud of him after Laurent hosted him on that first return visit.

segments.title: Maurice Durand's visit and a California trip
segments.summary: Maurice Durand came down unannounced; Russell and Manetta visited him in California.

segments.chapter: Players and bands of old New Orleans
segments.title: The Durand-Humphrey band era and the Newman family
segments.summary: Laurent recalls the Alamo and Music Box, a pianist and his young trumpeter son who later played in New York with Erskine Hawkins.

segments.chapter: Players and bands of old New Orleans
segments.title: Barney Bigard, Albert Nicholas and Dominique
segments.summary: He says he helped Albert Nicholas read music before he and Bigard left together, and mentions the Dominique cousins.

segments.chapter: Players and bands of old New Orleans
segments.title: The 150-piece band at the Regal Theater
segments.summary: Russell and Laurent mention Charlie Elgar directing a very large band at Chicago's Regal Theater.

segments.chapter: Players and bands of old New Orleans
segments.title: Manuel Perez outblowing Joe Oliver
segments.summary: Laurent says Manuel Perez was the best cornetist of his boyhood and describes him beating Joe Oliver at a wagon contest.

segments.chapter: Players and bands of old New Orleans
segments.title: The best dance bands and Perez's lineup
segments.summary: He rates Buddy Petit, Joe Oliver and Manuel Perez's bands, and lists the players Perez kept around his son.

segments.chapter: Players and bands of old New Orleans
segments.title: Missed meeting and his wife's illness
segments.summary: Russell and Laurent talk about missing each other, and his wife's long illness and hospital stays.

segments.chapter: Players and bands of old New Orleans
segments.title: Best trombonists and drummers of the old days
segments.summary: Laurent mentions Lowey Warner, Emanuel Ridgely, Zue Robertson and Vic Gaspar, and praises drummer Cantrell.

segments.chapter: Players and bands of old New Orleans
segments.title: Piano players of the period
segments.summary: He names Little Willie, Helen Edwards, Emma Barrett and others as the leading jazz pianists.

segments.chapter: Players and bands of old New Orleans
segments.title: Learning to play melody in a three-piece job
segments.summary: Playing with only piano and drums forced him to carry the melody; he plays Copenhagen as an example.

segments.chapter: Players and bands of old New Orleans
segments.title: Shaking the arm for a trilling effect
segments.summary: Russell asks whether he uses an Armstrong-like arm shake on the clarinet, which gives a trill effect.
